criteria.name: Introduction — Identifies ethical issues and broad links to engineering design; discusses the context of ethical issues in engineering organisations; identifies relevant stakeholders when considering the ethical issues.
criteria.reasoning: Three distinct ethical issues (risk-driven testing, treating data loss as harmless, conflict of interest/undisclosed defects) are linked to engineering design and organisational context (six-month cadence, revenue, decision authority). A stakeholder table gives interests and the decision each controls, including patients who cannot consent.

evidence.quote: First, test coverage is being set by the release calendar instead of by risk, which is a design-process decision made by the organisation
Table 1: Stakeholders, their interests and the decision each controls.

criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions on the ethical issues; draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: Genuine for-and-against arguments (time-to-market, learning, no defect-free product) are stated then rebutted with reasons rather than opinion. Conclusions on decision-making are targeted at several stakeholders: Rachel, management, the health department, the chip supplier and design engineers.

evidence.quote: The competitor argument assumes the buyer cannot tell the products apart; a health department that is told the failure rates can choose for itself
Rachel should withhold quality sign-off for the health contract, record the untested failure modes in writing and escalate to management.

criteria.name: Compelling Argument that supports conclusion — The report forms a compelling argument that justifies the conclusion; the body follows a logical structure, with linked paragraphs and content ordered to support the argument; arguments demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders.
criteria.reasoning: Logical flow: issues, stakeholder map, arguments for, arguments against, decision rule, option comparison, conclusion. The option table systematically allocates risk to each stakeholder, so the conclusion follows from the preceding argument.

evidence.quote: Options B and C respect every stakeholder's interests better than either extreme.
Table 2: Options for the health contract.

criteria.name: Research and Evidence — Arguments are substantiated with adequate references and qualitative/quantitative evidence; research demonstrates a balanced, in-depth understanding of the topic.
criteria.reasoning: Eight credible references support both qualitative reasoning and quantitative evidence across four relevant external cases (WannaCry, Therac-25, Pentium, Volkswagen), balanced by acknowledging where analogies do not transfer (WannaCry was an attack, Volkswagen was fraud).

evidence.quote: at least 81 of 236 hospital trusts in England were disrupted, an estimated 19,000 appointments were cancelled
when customers discovered it, Intel had to offer replacements and took a charge of US$475 million

criteria.name: Report Structure, Format and Language — The report includes appropriate sections serving their functions (abstract, introduction, body, and conclusion); maps, figures, tables, and visual elements are correctly used to support discussion; writing is grammatically correct, fluent, concise, easy to read and understand, and uses appropriate word choice; references are well-structured and appropriate, supporting the report’s motivations.
criteria.reasoning: All required sections serve their functions, with an abstract of roughly the required length, two informative tables and a flowchart used substantively. Prose is fluent, concise and largely error-free; IEEE references are consistently structured and relevant.

technical_issues.issue: WannaCry extent is usually reported as 80 of 236 trusts affected (NAO); '81 of 236' is a minor factual slip.

technical_issues.where: How should Rachel decide when to ship?
technical_issues.issue: States the failure rate 'has not been measured', but the scenario implies a known higher failure likelihood from partial testing; partial data versus full test coverage is not distinguished.

technical_issues.where: How should Rachel decide when to ship?
technical_issues.issue: Decision-rule step 2 equates 'tolerable' with 'no harm to people', which is stricter than standard risk-acceptance practice (AS ISO 31000) it cites.
Health-contract consequences are argued mainly by analogy to ransomware and radiotherapy cases rather than direct analysis of hospital/emergency-service failure modes.

overall: A strong, tightly argued report: explicit stakeholder and option analysis, a defensible decision rule, four well-used case studies and targeted, justified recommendations. Minor slips in one statistic and in characterising the known defect risk do not undermine the conclusion.

feedback.summary: Your report is a strong, tightly argued case: explicit stakeholder and option analysis, a defensible decision rule, four well-used case studies and targeted recommendations. All criteria are at Excellent. To sustain that level, tighten a few details: the WannaCry figure, the characterisation of the known defect risk, the decision-rule wording, and direct analysis of health-contract failure modes.
next_steps: Correct the WannaCry extent in 'Arguments against shipping' to 80 of 236 trusts affected (NAO) and check the 19,000 appointments figure against the same source.

In 'How should Rachel decide when to ship?', distinguish partial test data from full test coverage and reword decision-rule step 2 so 'tolerable' aligns with AS ISO 31000 risk-acceptance practice rather than 'no harm to people'.
In DISCUSSION, add direct analysis of hospital/emergency-service failure modes for the health contract instead of relying mainly on ransomware and radiotherapy analogies.

criteria.C1: You identify three distinct ethical issues—risk-driven testing, treating data loss as harmless, and conflict of interest/undisclosed defects—and link them to engineering design and organisational context (six-month cadence, revenue, decision authority). This meets the Excellent descriptor; to keep it there, ensure each stakeholder's interest is tied explicitly to one of the named issues.
criteria.C2: Your for-and-against arguments are genuine and rebutted with reasons, not opinion—the competitor argument in 'Arguments for shipping' is answered by the health department's ability to choose when told failure rates. This is Excellent; to sustain it, align decision-rule step 2 in 'How should Rachel decide when to ship?' with AS ISO 31000 risk acceptance.
criteria.C3: Your structure is logical—issues, stakeholder map, arguments for, arguments against, decision rule, option comparison, conclusion—and Table 2 allocates risk to each stakeholder so the conclusion follows from the argument. The option table and Figure 1 support the flow. This is Excellent; to keep it there, add direct health-contract failure-mode analysis in DISCUSSION so the conclusion rests on the scenario as well as the analogies.
criteria.C4: You use eight credible references and four external cases (WannaCry, Therac-25, Pentium, Volkswagen), balancing qualitative reasoning with quantitative evidence such as the US$475 million Pentium charge. You also acknowledge where analogies do not transfer. This is Excellent; to sustain it, correct the WannaCry extent to 80 of 236 trusts (NAO) and verify the 19,000 appointments figure against the same source.
criteria.C5: All required sections serve their functions, with an abstract of roughly the required length, two informative tables and Figure 1 used substantively. Prose is fluent, concise and largely error-free; IEEE references are consistently structured and relevant. This is Excellent; to keep it there, ensure the WannaCry statistic and decision-rule wording are corrected so the text and tables remain fully consistent.
